articleSummary: Newcastle disease (ND) remains endemic in Indonesia, which first described ND in 1926 and today hosts outbreaks in at least 15 provinces despite a general case decline over the past five years. articleSummary: Hepatitis refers to acute or chronic liver inflammation caused by viruses A–E or by alcohol, toxins, or autoimmune processes. It can be silent in early stages but, if untreated, progress to cirrhosis, liver failure, or liver cancer. Early signs include extreme fatigue, jaundice (yellow eyes/skin), dark urine, pale stools, right upper-quadrant abdominal pain, loss of appetite, nausea, and abdominal or leg swelling from fluid retention. Major causes: viral hepatitis A and E through contaminated water and unsanitary food; hepatitis B and C via infected blood, unsterilized needles, unsafe sex, and mother-to-child transmission. Alcoholic hepatitis, toxic drug-induced hepatitis, and autoimmune hepatitis are also important. Hepatitis B and C can remain asymptomatic for years; diagnosis uses liver-function tests (ALT/AST/bilirubin), screening (HBsAg, anti-HCV), viral-load testing (DNA/RNA), and imaging (ultrasound, FibroScan). Prevention emphasizes vaccination for A and B, clean water/food, avoiding alcohol, and avoiding self-medication. Early detection enables recovery; Areekode-based care notes emphasize timely management.

articleSummary: Invasive Aedes mosquitoes—Aedes aegypti (yellow fever mosquito) and Aedes albopictus (tiger mosquito)—transmit dengue, yellow fever, chikungunya, and Zika, with expansion from tropical regions to the Americas, Europe, and beyond. articleHeadline: Knowledge Nugget | Chandipura Virus: A silent viral threat behind India's recent outbreaks
articleSummary: Chandipura virus (CHPV) reemerges as a pediatric encephalitis pathogen in India. In the current outbreak, nine laboratory-confirmed CHPV deaths have been reported as of July 24: seven in Gujarat and two in Rajasthan; two Rajasthan children have died, triggering enhanced surveillance in Gujarat. CHPV is a member of the Rhabdoviridae family; vectors include Phlebotomine sandflies and Aedes aegypti; the virus resides in the salivary glands and is transmitted by bites, leading to encephalitis. Early CHPV infection presents with fever, body ache, and headache, and can progress to altered sensorium or seizures; retrospective reports note respiratory distress, bleeding, or anemia, with mortality often within 24–48 hours of hospitalization; children under 15 are most affected. First isolated in 1965 at Chandipura, Maharashtra. Major historical outbreaks occurred in 2003–04 (Maharashtra, northern Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh) with high case-fatality rates (Gujarat ~78%; Andhra Pradesh ~55%). Endemic to central India; outbreaks commonly occur in rural/tribal areas with higher sandfly populations.
notes: 記事はUPSC試験対策の知識解説記事だが、2026年7月時点での実際の集団発生（9名の検査確定死亡例）を報告しており、単なる歴史的解説にとどまらない現行イベントとして評価した。サシチョウバエ・ネッタイシマカを媒介とするため直接的なヒト-ヒト感染リスクは低いが、小児における高い致死率と監視体制強化の動きから注視が必要。

articleSummary: Brazilian wildcats such as puma, ocelot, jaguarundi, and jaguar face a critical situation from habitat loss, illegal wildlife trade, and human pressure across Brazil’s biomes. Fragmentation creates isolated habitat 'islands' that increase contact with domestic cats and dogs, elevating disease exposure and threatening genetic health. Brazil hosts 30 million house cats and 10 million strays, fueling wildcat spillover and hybridization risks. The Pampas cat (Leopardus munoai), endemic to the Pampas biome, is imperiled by pet theft, habitat loss, road threats, and disease exposure from domestic animals. A 2024 study identified exposure to FeLV, FPV, Canine Distemper (CDV), and Rabies. Rabies antibodies have been detected in jaguars in Pantanal and Emas National Park. Emerging threats include feline sporotrichosis (Sporothrix brasiliensis) and Bartonella henselae. Prevention requires mass vaccination of dogs and cats, habitat protection, and sustained disease surveillance and education to avert declines of Pampas cat and jaguar.
notes: 本記事は野生ネコ科動物の保全に関する環境ニュースであり、狂犬病・スポロトリコーシス等の病原体曝露は動物間のものでヒトへの感染事例は言及されていない。

articleHeadline: Andhra Pradesh to draw up action plan against zoonotic diseases
articleSummary: Andhra Pradesh will formulate a comprehensive action plan to prevent zoonotic diseases—transmitted from animals to humans—through early detection and coordinated surveillance. A three-day workshop in Vijayawada, organized by the State Health Department with support from the NCDC, CDC, and JHPIEGO, brought together officials from Health, Animal Husbandry, Forests, Environment, Agriculture, Fisheries, medical and veterinary experts, and partner institutions to identify high-priority diseases. An initial 45-disease list was reviewed, including scrub typhus, anthrax, histoplasmosis, dengue, Zika, yellow fever, COVID-19, and rabies. The plan will rank diseases by severity, public-health risk, and preventive feasibility, and, on completion, finalize a priority list with recommendations on prevention, surveillance, laboratory testing, and response strategies. Actions target strengthened surveillance in humans and animals, expanded diagnostic lab capacity, inter-departmental coordination, personnel training, and community awareness. Participants included Director of Animal Husbandry Damodar Naidu and NCDC Assistant Director Sukarma Tanwar.

articleSummary: Toxoplasmosis during pregnancy is caused by Toxoplasma gondii and can be transmitted to the fetus, risking preterm birth, intracranial calcifications, vision impairment, hearing loss, and developmental delays. Transmission risk increases with gestational age, but severe fetal disease is more likely with earlier maternal infection, while late infections more often transmit but cause milder presentations. In Brazil, prenatal screening includes serology to determine susceptibility or immunity; at HU-UFSCar in São Carlos, tests are repeated every two months to detect acute infection promptly and enable treatment. Amniocentesis may be used to assess amniotic fluid if infection is suspected. Treatment is coordinated by CAIC and HU-UFSCar. Prevention centers on hygiene and food safety: thoroughly cook meat, wash fruits and vegetables, wash hands, use potable water, avoid handling cat litter, and minimize contact with cat feces; pet cats do not pose significant risk if not infected. Early diagnosis and prenatal care are central.
